To put the pronoun in the right place: before the conjugated verb, attached to the infinitive.

Saturday, the end of February. Ilinca has come to visit for a long weekend. Matei takes her to the trattoria, where Giulia is waiting for them.
Ilinca, this is Giulia. Giulia, this is my sister.
At last! I know you from all of Matei's photos. Hi, Ilinca!
Hi! I know you too: my brother talks about you every day.
That's not true! I mean… sometimes.
Welcome, dear! Are you hungry? I've made ribollita. Do you know it?
No, I don't know it. What is it?
A Tuscan soup with bread and vegetables. I make it every winter. Sit down, I'll bring it to you right away.
Ilinca, did you know Matei has already learned to make ravioli?
Yes, I know! I saw the photo: he made them all broken!
They were the first ones! Now I can make them really well.
And you, Ilinca, can you cook?
No, not at all! Matei gave me a book of Tuscan recipes, but I haven't opened it yet.
Then tomorrow I'll teach you. Even children can make ribollita.
And tomorrow afternoon I'll take you to the Uffizi. I know an excellent guide: me!
(quietly, to Matei) I like her. Are you going to marry her?

The apostrophe links the words: "l'ho visto" = "lo vee-sto", in one breath. The H stays silent.
SC + e = "sh": co-NO-sce-re = "co-NO-she-re". But SC + o = "sk": co-NO-sco.
The i in "valigia" isn't read separately: va-LI-gia = "va-lee-ja".
Initial Z + ZZ inside a word: ZUP-pa (with "dz" or "ts" — both are heard in Italy), pa-LAT-tso.
The direct object pronoun answers the question "whom? / what?" and replaces the noun so you don't repeat it. As in Romanian: "Do you know Giulia? — Yes, I know HER."
Mi aspetti? (Will you wait for me?)
"Lo / la" become "l'" before a vowel or h: "L'aspetto" (I'm waiting for him / her), "L'ho visto". Li / le never take an apostrophe.
With "Lei" the imperative keeps the pronoun BEFORE: "Mi aspetti!" (Wait for me!) — but "Aspettami!" with tu.
When lo / la / li / le come before AVERE, the participle agrees with the pronoun (like an adjective):
With mi, ti, ci, vi the agreement is optional: "Giulia, ti ho vista / ti ho visto ieri" — both are correct.
This is why we had "l'ho cominciata" in chapter 10: "la relazione" is feminine, so the participle ends in -a.
In Romanian both can be "a ști / a cunoaște", but in Italian they are two different verbs:
facts: Sai che Matei è romeno?
things, from experience: Conosci la ribollita?
+ infinitive = to know how to: So nuotare.
to meet (in the past): Ho conosciuto Giulia a ottobre.
to find out (in the past): L'ho saputo ieri.
Trick: SAPERE is usually followed by che, dove, come, quando, se, or an infinitive. CONOSCERE is followed by a noun.
5. Neutral lo: Lo so, Non lo so
"Lo" can replace a whole clause. That's why Italians always say "Lo so" (I know it), not just "So":
Do you know there's a strike tomorrow? — Yes, I know.
Do you know I care about you?
And with "dire": "Te lo dico" (I'll tell you), "Chi l'ha detto?" (who said so?).
Do you drink coffee? — Yes, I drink it every morning.
Are you buying the tickets? — Yes, I'll buy them.
Where are the keys? I can't find them!
Did you see the tower? — Yes, I saw it.
Did you make ravioli? — Yes, I made them.
I want to invite her tomorrow.

Ilinca arrived on Thursday evening with an enormous suitcase. Matei waited for her at the airport for an hour because the flight was late. When he saw her, he hugged her tight: he hadn't seen her since Christmas.
In the suitcase there were loads of presents: Dad's pălincă, Mum's sarmale, Grandma's biscuits. Graziella tasted the sarmale and said: "I want to make them too! Will you teach me?"

On Friday morning Matei took Ilinca to the workshop. Professor Bellini greeted her with a bow and showed her the painting Matei was restoring: a small fifteenth-century Madonna. "Your brother treats her like a daughter," he said. Ilinca hadn't known the professor could smile.

On Saturday they played tourist. The Duomo? They saw it from the top, after four hundred and sixty-three steps. The Ponte Vecchio? They crossed it three times. The David? They looked at it for half an hour without speaking. In the evening they ordered a bistecca alla fiorentina, but Ilinca didn't finish it: it was bigger than the plate.

In the afternoon Giulia took them to the Uffizi. She knew every painting and every story. In front of Filippo Lippi's Madonna she stopped and told the story of the professor and his grandfather. Ilinca listened open-mouthed.

On Sunday Graziella gave Ilinca her first cooking lesson. Together they made ribollita. Ilinca chopped the vegetables (badly), burned the bread (a little) and added too much salt (a lot). But Pietro ate it all and said: "Delicious!" Pietro is a true gentleman.
On Monday morning, at the airport, Ilinca hugged everyone: Graziella, Pietro, Giulia. Then she took Matei aside.
"Listen, big brother. Giulia looks at you the way you look at your paintings. You know that, right?"
Matei went red. "I know," he said quietly. "But I don't know how to tell her."
Ilinca laughed. "You're a restorer. You know how to wait, how to look, how to find hidden colours. Use the same hands. And next time I come, I want an answer."
Then she disappeared beyond passport control, with her enormous suitcase, now full of oil, wine and Tuscan recipes.
